title: TextOp: Stream Updated Text into Closed-Loop Humanoid Motion
content_lines: Source: [arXiv:2602.07439v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07439v1). Code mapping uses the pinned official TextOp revision linked by the Chinese page.

> **Bottom line:** TextOp generates short G1 reference-motion chunks from current text plus recent robot-skeleton history, then tracks them with a separate 50 Hz policy trained on both MoCap and generated motion. Text can change without resetting the execution state; this is an interface for streamed commands, not evidence of environment-aware motion safety.
## Engineering problem

One-shot text-to-motion loses phase when a command changes mid-execution. Directly joining generated clips can discontinuously change root pose, support foot, or joint velocity, while a tracker trained only on MoCap may fail on generator-specific transitions.
## Method

A 6.25 Hz diffusion Transformer generates an eight-frame future from the latest two-frame robot-skeleton history and current CLIP text embedding, using five denoising steps and classifier-free guidance. A separate PPO tracker executes the reference at 50 Hz on 29-DoF G1. Updating text changes the embedding but preserves motion history, and mixed MoCap/generated training adapts the tracker to its actual upstream distribution.
## Key figures
![Figures 2-3: streaming generator, aligned data, and tracker](../assets/textop-2602.07439v1/figure-2-3-streaming.jpg)
Figures 2-3 separate the text-update event, 6.25 Hz generation, and 50 Hz tracking clocks; the tracker closes the physical loop between generated chunks.
![Tables I-II: 30-second hardware trials and latency](../assets/textop-2602.07439v1/table-1-2-hardware.jpg)

Table I reports explicit 30-second trial denominators. Table II separates 7.64 ms text encoding, 29.63 ms generation, 2.15 ms tracking, and 0.73±0.10 s human-perceived response; the last number is not low-level control latency.
![Tables III-IV: representation and tracker data distribution](../assets/textop-2602.07439v1/table-3-4-representation.jpg)

Tables III-IV show that representation and tracker training distribution are part of the interface. Mixed training helps on generated motion, while MoCap-only performs best on the unseen SnapMoGen distribution reported in Table V.
## Decisive evidence

Random streamed command combinations succeed in 16/20 hardware trials; cyclic punch and guitar/violin trials report 10/10, while wave reports 8/10. These denominators support interactive execution under the tested vocabulary, but not arbitrary text, obstacle avoidance, or long-duration autonomy.
## Paper-to-implementation mapping

At pinned commit `ef6555fb174c9b5c44945a62c7ffc77b5ddbbf22`, `MotionDAR._gen_motion` retains tail history, `_update_text_embedding` changes text without resetting the chain, and `_publish_motion_block` hands generated references to the tracker. `ClassifierFreeWrapper`, `generate_next_motion`, and `DenoiserTransformer.forward` expose the CFG and history-conditioned generation path. The repository warns that the latest paper code and dataset were not yet updated, so commit behavior must not be treated as a complete v1 artifact.
## Limits and evidence boundary

The authors state that TextOp does not perceive geometry and cannot adapt motion to obstacles, terrain, or dynamic objects. Open text is bounded by CLIP/BABEL vocabulary and training motion; autoregressive drift, ambiguous commands, unsafe amplitude, and unreported tail latency remain independent risks. The small random-combination denominator and qualitative push tests do not prove long-horizon reliability.
## Bounded engineering takeaway

Reuse the architecture as `streaming short-horizon generator + separately validated tracker`, and treat generator output as an untrusted reference. Keep command parsing, reachability, collision, joint-limit, velocity, timeout, and emergency-stop supervision outside the language model and generator.
## Reproduction checklist

Lock BABEL/AMASS filtering, GMR version, two-frame history, eight-frame horizon, five denoising steps, CFG scale, generated/MoCap mix, high/low-level clocks, and pinned code revision. Timestamp text submission, embedding update, generation start/end, block publish/receive, and first visible motion. Test similar, periodic-to-aperiodic, and support-conflicting command switches; report semantic success, root/support continuity, tracking termination, tail latency, refusals, falls, limit interventions, and long-stream drift separately.
